observation_summary: The RegulaFalsiSolver fails with a TooManyEvaluationsException because the algorithm enters an infinite loop where it repeatedly updates the same bound without making progress, eventually exhausting the evaluation limit.
hypothesis: The Regula Falsi algorithm, when implemented with limited floating-point precision, can get stuck in a state where the update formula produces the same value repeatedly. The fix introduces a check to detect this stagnation and forces an update to the search interval to ensure progress.
prediction: The code will include a conditional check within the solver loop to detect if the new approximation 'x' is identical to the previous bound 'x1'. If so, it will manually adjust the interval bounds to force the algorithm to continue.
experiment_rationale: The fix diff shows the addition of a 'REGULA_FALSI' case in the solver's update logic that explicitly checks 'if (x == x1)' and then modifies 'x0' and 'f0'. This confirms that the root cause was a failure in the algorithmic progression logic, which is now corrected by adding a recovery step.
reasoning_summary: The bug is an algorithmic failure where the standard Regula Falsi procedure fails to converge due to floating-point limitations. The fix modifies the computational procedure by adding a recovery step (forcing an interval update) when stagnation is detected. This is a classic algorithmic correction to ensure the procedure terminates correctly, fitting the 'Algorithm/Method' category.
evidence_used: The fix_diff_oracle shows the addition of a REGULA_FALSI case that modifies x0 and f0 when x == x1.
The bug report comments from Gilles Sadowski and Luc Maisonobe confirm that the issue is a known limitation of the Regula Falsi algorithm's convergence in finite precision.
The failing test stack trace shows a TooManyEvaluationsException, indicating an infinite loop or excessive iterations.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the fix adds a check (if x == x1), the primary purpose is to modify the algorithmic progression (the update formula) to ensure convergence, not just to validate input or prevent an error.
This is a local procedural correction to an existing algorithm, not a design-level capability gap or a missing class/object.
